newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-PLO summit closes in on Hebron deal - U.S.
newsitem.headline: Israel-PLO summit closes in on Hebron deal - U.S.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian leaders failed at a summit to wrap up a Hebron deal in time for Christmas Eve on Tuesday but a U.S. envoy reported "real progress" towards the long-elusive accord.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat met for 3-1/2 hours at the Israeli-Gaza border in a U.S.-mediated bid to close a deal that would give Palestinians self-rule in the West Bank town.

"We don't have an agreement yet but it's very clear that this was a meeting that was extremely productive," U.S. President Bill Clinton's Middle East envoy Dennis Ross told reporters. "They have made real progress."
"They have in fact made the kind of progress that takes us closer to agreement," Ross said.
He said the two leaders, who last met 12 weeks ago, had instructed their negotiating teams to meet again on Christmas morning on Wednesday and that Netanyahu and Arafat would meet again soon.

"The atmosphere was very productive. For the first time since the talks started, there was consistency with the agreements signed (with Israel's previous Labour government)," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters.
Arafat's spokesman Marwan Kanafani said the two leaders would meet again once all of the remaining issues were resolved.

Israel and the PLO had accused each other of foot-dragging in talks on an Israeli troop redeployment that would give Arafat's Palestinian Authority control of 80 percent of Hebron. The Israeli newspaper Maariv said the army, once given the green light, could execute the pullout within half an hour.

Israeli media had speculated the sides could wrap up an accord by Christmas Day as a "holiday present" to Clinton, who has nudged forward the difficult talks between Israel and the PLO since they signed a landmark deal in 1993.

Netanyahu has said he would sign an agreement only if it guaranteed the safety of the 400 Jewish settlers who live among more than 100,000 Arabs in Hebron, a longtime hotbed of Moslem and Jewish militancy seized by Israel with the rest of the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East war.

Arabs view the withdrawal, promised by Israel's former Labour government, as an acid test of Netanyahu's intentions following his election in May on a promise to take a tough line on the security of Israelis.

The talks, which seemed near ruin in recent weeks, came to life over the weekend with the arrival of Ross, who shuttled between Israel, Gaza and Egypt to try to broker a deal. Ross's last mission collapsed in October.

In Egypt on Tuesday, visiting Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai promised Israel would continue talks on all pending issues following a Hebron deal. Arabs have voiced fear that Netanyahu plans to go no further with negotiations.
After coming to power in June, Netanyahu had resisted even meeting Arafat, once vilified by the Israeli leader's Likud party as a "master terrorist".
The unexpected progress towards a deal sent shock waves through Hebron's Jewish population.
"We're crossing our fingers that this agreement, which, Heaven forbid, will bring catastrophe on the Jewish community ...will not be signed," Hebron resident Moshe Ben-Zimra told Israel Radio.

Palestinian officials have said Israel has dropped its insistence on having the right of "hot pursuit" of Palestinian suspects into PLO-held areas, accepting instead existing language in the Hebron handover agreement signed in 1995.
Hebron is the last Palestinian town due to be given self-rule under Israeli-PLO peace deals dating back to 1993.

Netanyahu and Arafat last met at an emergency summit in Washington called by Clinton to ease tensions following clashes and gun battles that claimed the lives of 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis in September.
The bloodshed erupted over Netanyahu's opening of a tunnel near Islamic holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem.
